title: Seed and stone split open
hook: Allah splits the grain and the date-stone, brings the living from the dead (6:95)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stars, Ibrahim's search in its full setting. Your line was love what doesn't set. Did you catch the sunset? Today, from the sky down into the soil. Day four hundred one.

Pick up a date pit after you've eaten the fruit. It's hard as a pebble, dry, with a little groove down one side. You could keep it in a drawer for a year and it would look exactly the same. It looks finished. Dead, even. And yet bury it in warm, wet soil, wait, and one day that stone cracks from the inside and a green shoot pushes out. Nobody pried it open. Surah six, verse ninety-five, points straight at that moment and says who did.
screen: `A DATE PIT, HARD AS A PEBBLE.` → `IT LOOKS FINISHED.` → `IT CRACKS FROM THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The verse says Allah is the one who splits the grain and the date-stone. Two Arabic words carry it. Habb: a grain, a seed, the kind you'd scatter for planting. And nawa: the hard pit inside a date, the stone. The verb is falaqa, to split, to cleave open. Its root names the daybreak too. The very next verse calls Allah faliq al-isbah, the one who splits open the dawn, and the second-to-last surah of the Qur'an, al-Falaq, takes its name from the same root. Seed and morning: two things that open from inside, on time, every time. Then the verse goes further: He brings the living out of the dead, and the dead out of the living. Commentators gave many examples. The green plant out of the dry seed, and the dry seed out of the plant again. The chick out of the egg. And, some said, a believer born to people who didn't believe, and the reverse. The verse ends with a question: such is Allah, so how are you turned away? It's an argument made with things you can hold. And the Prophet ﷺ cared about planting. A hadith in Bukhari says that when someone plants a tree and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for the one who planted it. Another report, in the Musnad of Ahmad, says that even if the Hour is coming and you have a palm shoot in your hand, plant it. A seed is a small act of trust. You can't make it split. You only put it where it can.
screen: `HABB AND NAWA — GRAIN AND STONE.` · `FALAQA — TO SPLIT OPEN, LIKE DAWN.` · `THE LIVING FROM THE DEAD.` · `PLANT IT ANYWAY.` · then, large: `THE SEED SPLITS.`

segments.voice: If you have a seed, a pit, a bean or a grain of rice nearby, hold it in your palm. If not, picture one. Feel how hard it is, how finished it looks. Breathe. Imagine it underground, in the dark, and the slow moment when it cracks. If you can, plant it today: a pot, a cup of soil, a patch of ground. If not, plant the intention: find a spot this week. The bell holds the time.
Falaq, splitting: the same root as the dawn breaking open. Allah splits the grain and the date-stone, and the dawn, and brings the living from the dead. Today's word.
Your line: the seed splits. Today, plant something, or water something already planted, and leave the splitting to Allah. Day four hundred one.

howItsDone: Muslims read 6:95–99 as signs in agriculture and the sky; planting trees is widely encouraged as ongoing charity, following hadith in Bukhari and the Musnad of Ahmad.

original.note: Arabic: the splitter of the grain and the date-stone (6:95).

trapdoor: what you thought: God makes plants grow.
what it means: Allah cracks open what looks finished, seed and stone and dawn alike, and brings life out of what looks dead.
what a scholar hears: f-l-q links 6:95, faliq al-isbah in 6:96 and surah 113, al-Falaq; commentators read the living-from-dead pair both botanically and spiritually.
